# Veidekke ASA (VEI.OL) — A Deep Dive on Management and the Setup

*Prepared for the investment committee. No earnings-call transcript was bundled with this name; the analysis below draws on Veidekke's published Q4 2025 / full-year 2025 results (released February 12, 2026), the Q1 2026 report (released May 7, 2026), the company's spring 2026 market update, and its stated 2030 targets, all retrieved from the web and dated where it matters.*

Veidekke is one of Scandinavia's largest construction and civil-engineering groups, based in Norway with sizeable operations in Sweden. It builds homes and commercial buildings (its "Construction" / Bygg arm), builds roads, rail and other heavy infrastructure (its "Infrastructure" / Anlegg arm, split Norway and Sweden), and runs an asphalt and aggregates industrial business. It is run as a low-capital, project-execution business: it carries almost no net debt, pays out most of its earnings as dividends, and earns unusually high returns on the small amount of capital it does employ.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story Veidekke has told over the past two years is a steady, unflashy one: *fix the margin, hold the discipline, let the cycle come back.* After the 2022–2023 cost-inflation shock that squeezed every Nordic contractor, management's central message has been operational improvement rather than expansion — better project selection, better capacity utilisation, and tighter risk control on fixed-price work. That message has held remarkably constant.

The most recent inflection is genuinely positive. Coming out of full-year 2025 (reported February 2026), management shifted from "we are repairing profitability" to "the market is turning." The company now guides to roughly 5% activity growth in 2026 and 4% in 2027, with the recovery led by residential and small-housing construction — the very segment that was hit hardest in the downturn. By the Q1 2026 report (May 2026), that confidence was backed by hard order intake: the 12-month order backlog was up 8% year over year, with a "particularly strong book-to-bill in Bygg [Construction]," and asphalt season bookings rose to roughly 775,000 tonnes on national and county road contracts (from 640,000 a year earlier).

What has *not* changed — and this is the crux for a value committee — is the valuation framing. Nothing in the narrative arc suggests a hidden, mispriced asset or a coming corporate event. This is an operationally improving cyclical at the upswing of its cycle, telling a clean and credible story that the market already hears.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The screener metrics on this name are partly corrupted and must be read with care before testing any claim against them.

| Management / screener claim | The actual financials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "We improved profitability across all business areas in 2025" | Pre-tax profit NOK 2,057M in 2025, up 22% from NOK 1,683M; EBT margin 4.8% vs 4.1% in 2024; net income NOK 1.55B vs 1.26B; EPS 11.5 vs 9.3 (+23.7%) | **Holds.** The margin repair is real and broad-based, corroborated by the multi-year trajectory (net income up every year 2023→2025). |
| Screener: "Gross margin 100.0% (expanding)" | A data artifact. Contractors book revenue net of subcontractors; the feed mislabels this as a 100% gross margin. | **Does not hold up — discard.** The peer file flags the same artifact. Use net margin (~3.6%) and EBT margin (4.8%), which are normal-to-good for construction. |
| Screener: "Fair Value 14.0, Margin of Safety −99%, P/FCF 96x" | Downstream of the same artifact and a single trailing-FCF quirk. On real earnings (EPS ~11.5–11.7) at ~NOK 180, the price-to-earnings ratio is ~15.6x — a normal multiple, not 96x. | **Does not hold up — discard.** Every per-method margin-of-safety reads −100%, which is the model failing on bad inputs, not a genuine 99% overvaluation. |
| "Capital-efficient growth; strong balance sheet" | Net interest-bearing *position* of about NOK 4.6B (net cash) at Q1 2026, up from NOK 2.7B a year earlier; Q1 operating cash flow ~NOK 900M; the live correction in our inputs recomputes net cash at about NOK 4.36B. ROE 37.2%, ROIC 20.0%. | **Holds, and is the single best fact here.** This is a debt-free, cash-generative, high-return contractor — genuinely higher quality than most Nordic peers (Skanska ROIC ~12%, NCC ~10%). |
| "Order backlog supports the growth outlook" | 12-month backlog +8% YoY at Q1 2026; consistent 6–8% activity-growth trend | **Holds.** Forward visibility is improving, consistent with the 2026/2027 guide. |

The honest read: where the *narrative* is testable against clean numbers (margin repair, balance-sheet strength, order growth, returns on capital), it holds up well. Where the *screener* makes this look like a screaming value name (96x price-to-free-cash-flow, −99% margin of safety, a NOK 14 fair value against a NOK 191 price), the screener is simply wrong — these are artifacts, not a thesis.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising.** With no transcript bundled, this is inferred from the published reports and guidance, but the direction is unambiguous. Through 2024 the language was defensive and repair-oriented (capacity, discipline, project selection). By the February 2026 full-year report the company explicitly called a cyclical turn ("moderate upturn from 2026") and put numbers on it (5% growth in 2026, 4% in 2027). The Q1 2026 report then validated the optimism with a strong book-to-bill rather than walking it back. The shift is from defensive to cautiously offensive — but "cautiously" is the operative word; this is not a management team promising a step-change.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium-to-High.** The financials show earnings beats in 5 of the last 7 quarters (about 71%), and the multi-year delivery is clean: profit and margin both rose in 2024 and again in 2025, exactly as the "improvement programme" promised. The 2030 framework — long-term pre-tax margin above 5%, revenue growth ~2.5 points above the market, and a dividend policy of distributing more than 70% of earnings per share — is specific and conservative rather than promotional. Management tends to set achievable targets and hit them. The main credibility caveat is structural, not behavioural: construction earnings are cyclical and fixed-price project risk can turn a good year into a write-down year, so even an honest team's guidance carries cycle risk.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The recurring tension is valuation, not operations. The street's own consensus recommendation on the stock is "sell," with an average twelve-month price target (around NOK 184–188) barely above the current price (~NOK 180) — analysts like the company and dislike the price. The pressure point a buyer must answer is simple: at ~15.6x earnings and roughly 86% of the way up its 52-week range, sitting above its 200-day average, what is left to capture in a contractor whose own guidance is "moderate" growth? There is no segment the market is ignoring and no asset it is missing.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 Margin repair delivered and broad-based (EBT margin 4.8%, +22% pre-tax profit in 2025).
🟢 Fortress balance sheet: ~NOK 4.4–4.6B net cash, essentially no debt, Altman-Z solvency 3.8.
🟢 Best-in-class returns for the peer set: ROIC ~20%, ROE ~37%.
🟢 Order backlog +8% and a cyclical recovery the company can now point to in its own bookings.

🔴 Valuation, full stop. The stock is rich versus its Scandinavian construction peers (AF Gruppen typically 8–12x free cash flow; Veidekke screens far above on any cash-flow multiple), and it sits near a 52-week high with the street rating it "sell."
🔴 The only discrete catalyst — the NOK 11.25 per-share dividend — has already been paid (ex-dividend May 7, 2026; paid May 20, 2026). The income event the yield-focused base was waiting for is behind us, not ahead.
🔴 Cyclical and fixed-price risk: a Nordic construction recovery is real but fragile, rate-sensitive (the Norwegian and Swedish rate path matters), and one large troubled project can dent a year.
🔴 The "deep value" label on this candidate is an artifact. Every genuine valuation method on clean inputs says fairly-to-richly valued, not cheap.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most important "hidden" signal is what the corrected inputs reveal: the screener's deep-value flag is built on a broken gross-margin field and a single trailing-FCF distortion, and the only model that fired (enterprise value to gross profit) is, as the peer note says, "a loose signal" on a margin-compressed contractor. Strip those away and there is no concealed cheapness. The genuinely under-appreciated fact is the *quality* of the balance sheet and returns — but quality is not the same as a mispricing, and the market is already paying a peer-premium multiple precisely because it sees that quality.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STABLE** — arguably strengthening operationally, but stable as an investment proposition. Veidekke is a well-run, debt-free, high-return Nordic contractor at the early-to-mid stage of a cyclical recovery, trading at a full peer-premium multiple near its 52-week high, with its one discrete catalyst (the dividend) already paid.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **this is not a deep-value special situation; it is a quality cyclical at a fair-to-rich price with no live catalyst.** Any position is a bet on the Nordic construction cycle continuing and the premium multiple holding — not on a discount closing. There is no margin of safety to lean on if the cycle stalls or a project goes wrong.

On the economic moat: Veidekke's advantage is a **scale-cost and local-execution edge** (regional density in asphalt and infrastructure, brand and relationships in a relationship-driven bid market) — real but **narrow**, the normal moat of a strong contractor, not a wide structural fortress. Construction is a low-margin, competitively-bid, commoditised-service industry; the company's high returns come from running it unusually well and keeping capital light, not from pricing power. The moat is **stable** (returns are high and steady, not eroding). There is **no terminal secular threat**: construction demand is cyclical, not structurally shrinking, and no technology or channel shift is collapsing this business's terminal value — the risk here is cyclical and valuation, not a melting base. No secular-decline theme applies.

bull_thesis: Veidekke is a genuinely well-run Scandinavian contractor that did exactly what it said it would do, and the second quarter of 2026 was its best evidence yet. Back in 2020 the company set a single public promise: put profitability ahead of growth and reach a 5% pre-tax profit margin (profit before tax divided by revenue) by 2025. It scored itself in the fourth-quarter 2025 report published on 12 February 2026: revenue up 13% over five years, from NOK 38.1 billion to NOK 43.1 billion, while pre-tax profit rose 81%, from NOK 1.1 billion to NOK 2.1 billion, lifting the margin from 3.0% to 4.8%. By the twelve months to 30 June 2026 the margin was 5.0% — the promise, kept. The second quarter itself, reported on 14 August 2026, showed revenue of NOK 12.3 billion (up 9% on the year), pre-tax profit of NOK 670 million (up 25%), and a 5.4% margin, with every one of the five divisions improving both revenue and profit. Behind that sits a record order book of NOK 55.3 billion at 30 June, up from NOK 49.2 billion a year earlier and NOK 47.3 billion at year-end, of which NOK 30.5 billion converts to revenue within twelve months. Quarterly order intake of NOK 17.9 billion included a NOK 5.5 billion contract for the E134 Oslofjord Link from the Norwegian Public Roads Administration. The balance sheet is the other half of the case: net interest-bearing assets of NOK 3.65 billion at 30 June, and that is after paying out NOK 1.5 billion of dividend during the quarter, with NOK 3.0 billion of committed bank facilities entirely undrawn. The stated policy is to distribute more than 70% of earnings per share, and the company has: NOK 9.00 per share for 2024 and NOK 11.25 for 2025, which at NOK 210 is a yield of about 5.4%. Management is using the cash rather than hoarding it — buying local asphalt and aggregates businesses at strikingly low prices, including Nord Vei & Asfalt in Troms on 27 April 2026 for NOK 87 million, a business that made NOK 38 million of operating profit on NOK 236 million of revenue in 2025, a little over two times operating profit. That matters strategically: asphalt, quarries and haulage radius are the one part of a contractor that has real local pricing power, and Veidekke is steadily buying more of it. Over the last twelve months asphalt and aggregates earned a 6.7% pre-tax margin and Denmark 10.2%, against 4.6% in Norwegian civil engineering — the mix is drifting toward the better businesses. The conditions the bull case needs: that the record order book converts at the current margin rather than at the lower margin of the work being replaced; that Swedish building, at a 2.7% margin over the last twelve months, is finally fixed toward the 4% the company thinks it should earn; that bitumen costs stay passed through; and that the market keeps paying thirteen to fifteen times for it. If all four hold, earnings power of roughly NOK 15 to NOK 16 per share by 2027 at fourteen times, plus the net cash, is worth about NOK 235 a share — and the shareholder collects a 5-6% dividend while waiting.
bear_thesis: The bear case is not that Veidekke is a bad company. It is that you are being asked to pay a top-of-range price for a top-of-range margin, and that the number which flagged this stock as cheap is a measurement error. Start with the error. Our screener shows a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 9.8 times, trailing free cash flow of NOK 4.44 billion, and a model-derived fair value of NOK 350 — and all three inherit the same flaw. In 2025 Veidekke reported NOK 2.89 billion of free cash flow, but that figure contains a NOK 766 million working-capital inflow (customer money, not earned profit), charges only NOK 399 million of capital spending against NOK 1,099 million of depreciation, and excludes NOK 509 million of lease payments booked in the financing section of the cash-flow statement. Correct all three and sustainable free cash is close to reported net profit — roughly NOK 1.6 to NOK 1.7 billion — so the honest multiple of distributable cash at NOK 210 is about seventeen times, not under ten. Even the second quarter's strong operating cash flow of NOK 856 million is disclosed by the company itself as helped by a one-off NOK 550 million advance received on signing the Oslofjord Link contract. On earnings the picture is the same: NOK 210 is 16.8 times the last twelve months' earnings per share of NOK 12.50, or roughly fifteen times once the NOK 27 per share of net cash is set aside. That would be an ordinary multiple for a business with pricing power. Veidekke does not have much: outside asphalt and quarries, it wins work bid by bid at 3 to 5 percent margins, which is the honest measure of its bargaining position. The 56% return on equity is not evidence to the contrary — it is arithmetic on a 13% equity ratio, because customers and suppliers fund the projects. And the margin being capitalised is the best in the company's recorded history. Our own screener puts it 1.27 standard deviations from its historic peak; the ten-year range is 3 to 4.5 percent. Denmark at 10.2% and Infrastructure Sweden at 5.9% over the last twelve months are both well above their own long-run levels, and Infrastructure Sweden's order book fell 19% in local currency year on year — the best margin sitting on the worst backlog. Three specific things can break it. First, bitumen: the second-quarter report gives a full paragraph to Middle East turmoil pushing up oil and therefore bitumen, states that price rises squeeze public asphalt budgets and private demand, and concedes 'uncertainty about asphalt volumes in 2026'; the contracts allow volume to move up or down by 15%. Second, one project: the group's entire equity is NOK 2.6 billion and its largest new contract is NOK 5.5 billion of technically demanding subsea tunnelling — contractors do not die of slow decline, they die of one job. Third, the multiple: the same shares traded between NOK 170.80 and NOK 197.60 during the second quarter and closed the quarter at NOK 189.60, with a 52-week low of NOK 152.60. Nothing structural stops them going back. If margins revert to the 4.1% of 2024 and the market pays ten times, the shares are worth about NOK 105. That is the risk being taken for an upside that, on today's segment earnings, the price has already reached.
consensus_delta: There are two disagreements with the market here and they point in opposite directions, which is why the answer is a pass rather than a short. The first disagreement is in the company's favour and it is about the near-term numbers. Analyst coverage of this share is extremely thin — the estimate data carries only two forecasters — and they have been running behind the print. Their 2025 consensus earnings per share was NOK 10.22 against NOK 11.50 actually delivered, a 12% miss. For 2026 they carry NOK 12.41, but the first half already produced NOK 3.80 against NOK 2.80 a year earlier, a 36% increase, and the second half of the year is seasonally where this company makes its money. On an unchanged second-half growth rate the full year lands nearer NOK 13.30 to NOK 13.50. So near-term estimates are more likely to go up than down, and anyone expecting a disappointing print in November is probably wrong. The second disagreement is against the company and it is the one that decides the capital call. It is not about earnings at all — it is about what those earnings are worth. Consensus has revenue reaching NOK 51.3 billion by 2028 and earnings per share of NOK 13.79, which is barely 3.5% annual growth from the 2026 level, and at NOK 210 the market is paying fifteen times that, net of cash, for a business whose margin is already the best in its recorded history. The market assumption embedded in that price is that a 5% pre-tax margin is the new normal rather than the top of a range. The evidence says otherwise: the ten-year history runs at 3 to 4.5 percent, our screener puts the current margin 1.27 standard deviations from its historic peak, Denmark at 10.2% and Infrastructure Sweden at 5.9% over the last twelve months are both far above their own long-run levels, and Infrastructure Sweden's order book is down 19% in local currency — the highest margin sitting on the fastest-shrinking backlog. A second market assumption is embedded in how this name reached our screen at all: the reported free cash flow of NOK 4.44 billion, and the 9.8 times cash-flow multiple derived from it, are not distributable cash. They contain a NOK 766 million working-capital inflow, charge NOK 399 million of capital spending against NOK 1,099 million of depreciation, and exclude NOK 509 million of lease payments booked below the line. Corrected, the multiple of sustainable cash is about seventeen times. The market is not looking the wrong way on this company. If anything, it is looking at it rather carefully, which is why the shares sit at a 52-week high.
forcing_function: There is no event that forces the market to re-rate these shares upward, because the re-rating already happened. The dates that matter now are tests of a best-ever margin rather than catalysts for it. The third-quarter 2026 results are due in early November (the equivalent 2025 report was published on 6 November 2025) and will show whether the asphalt season's 17% volume gain survived contact with higher bitumen costs — that is the single most informative print in the next six months. The full-year 2026 results are due in mid-February 2027 (the 2025 equivalent was 12 February 2026) and will carry the board's dividend proposal under the more-than-70%-of-earnings policy; on a full-year figure near NOK 13.30 that implies something in the region of NOK 12 to NOK 13 per share, payable after the annual general meeting in early May 2027. Veidekke also publishes a Scandinavian contracting-market outlook twice a year on its own website, which is the closest thing this company offers to guidance. The genuine forcing function on the downside is different in kind and has no date attached: a single loss-making project. The group's entire equity is NOK 2.6 billion and its largest new contract, the NOK 5.5 billion E134 Oslofjord Link subsea tunnel, is more than twice that. Contractors re-rate violently on one job, in either direction, and nothing in the current disclosure lets an outsider judge how that risk is contained.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months contain no crisis, but they do contain a reliable de-rating window and two live cost pressures. The reliable window is seasonal and structural. Veidekke's first quarter is close to breakeven every single year, because asphalt is not laid in a Norwegian winter: Infrastructure Norway lost NOK 207 million before tax in the first quarter of 2026 and NOK 189 million in the first quarter of 2025, and group earnings per share for the first quarter of 2026 were NOK 0.10 against minus NOK 0.20 a year before. A share trading at nearly seventeen times trailing earnings has to walk through that print every February to May, and it does so immediately after the full-year dividend has been declared but before it has been paid. The first live pressure is bitumen, the oil-derived binder in asphalt. The second-quarter report devotes a paragraph to it: Middle East turmoil has pushed up oil and energy prices and therefore bitumen; public-sector contracts contain adjustment mechanisms that only 'largely' cover it; price rises squeeze public asphalt budgets and private demand; and the company states plainly that there is uncertainty about asphalt volumes for 2026. Veidekke has contracted just over 770,000 tonnes in this year's public tenders, well up on last year, but those contracts allow volumes to move 15% either way. With Brent around NOK-equivalent highs and the Hormuz situation re-escalated as of the mid-August market read, this is a real and dated squeeze on the single most profitable part of the group, and it will be visible in the third-quarter report in early November — the quarter that contains the peak of the paving season. The second pressure is the cost of money. Long-term interest rates are at a nineteen-year high, and Veidekke's own risk section says higher rates are cutting the financial capacity of both private and public clients, producing weak new-home sales and deferred or redesigned projects; management still expects construction market conditions to remain challenging. That does not hit the order book already signed, but it decides what replaces it. Finally, cash. The net position fell from NOK 4.02 billion at year-end to NOK 3.65 billion at 30 June after the NOK 1.5 billion dividend, and the second quarter's operating inflow was helped by a NOK 550 million one-off advance on the Oslofjord Link. As that project consumes its advance and the big civil works burn working capital, the cash figure that makes the balance sheet look impregnable will drift lower — not dangerously, but enough that anyone underwriting the full NOK 27 a share of net cash as permanent will be disappointed. There is no debt wall: total interest-bearing liabilities are NOK 170 million and NOK 3.0 billion of bank facilities sit undrawn.
positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling opportunity here, and that is itself the finding. The share register is built to sit still. As at 30 June 2026, OBOS, a Norwegian housing cooperative, held 19.5% and the state-linked Folketrygdfondet 9.8% — nearly 30% in two hands that do not trade. The ten largest holders account for 49.3%, foreign ownership is only 17.7%, and roughly 10% of the company is owned by its own employees. Just 4.6 million shares changed hands in the whole of the second quarter, against 135 million outstanding. This is a domestic, income-oriented, long-duration register: it will not panic into your bid, and it will not squeeze a short either. The one mechanical scenario that would move it is a dividend cut. Veidekke's stated policy is to distribute more than 70% of earnings per share, and it has been paying closer to 100% — NOK 11.25 for 2025 against earnings of NOK 11.50. A significant share of the register owns this specifically for that yield, so a cut, which would only come from a large loss-making project or a genuine margin break, would produce real mechanical selling from income funds. That is the entry this name is most likely to hand you, and it is not on the calendar. The practical conclusion for timing: do not wait for a wash-out that the ownership structure cannot produce. If this is ever bought, it will be bought into a bad print, not into a liquidation.
moderator_conclusion: Pass for now — a good business at a full price. Almost everything about Veidekke's operating record is admirable, and the forensic review found no reason to distrust the accounts: the company set a public five-year target in 2020 to lift its pre-tax profit margin to 5%, deliberately gave up growth to get there, and delivered 4.8% in 2025 and 5.0% over the twelve months to June 2026. Every division improved in the second quarter of 2026, the order book is a record NOK 55.3 billion, there is NOK 3.65 billion of net cash after a NOK 1.5 billion dividend, and management discloses its own soft spots — the one-off cash advance, the earn-out reversal, the acquisition contribution to revenue, the too-low Swedish margin and the missed safety target — rather than burying them. That earns a high credibility mark. The problem is entirely one of price, and it starts with the reason this name reached the screen at all. The 9.8-times free-cash-flow signal is a measurement error: strip out the working-capital inflow, charge depreciation-level capital spending instead of the NOK 399 million actually spent, and put the NOK 509 million of lease payments back where they belong, and sustainable free cash is close to reported profit — about seventeen times the current price, not under ten. The model-derived fair value of NOK 350 inherits the same flaw and should be discarded. On corrected numbers, NOK 210 is 16.8 times the last twelve months' earnings of NOK 12.50, or roughly fifteen times net of the NOK 27 a share of net cash, for a company earning the best margin in its recorded history in a business where work is won bid by bid at 3 to 5 percent. Valuing the divisions separately on normalised margins gives NOK 160 a share; valuing them on today's margins with a generous multiple and the full cash gives NOK 209 — which is to say the market price already contains the good case. The adverse case, a reversion to 2024 margins at ten times, is NOK 105. Reading this against the current market backdrop reinforces rather than changes the call: this is not a thesis that depends on rate cuts, and its driver — Scandinavian construction demand and Norwegian public works budgets — is genuinely independent of the crowded macro trades, which is a point in its favour. But long-term interest rates at a nineteen-year high raise the discount rate on precisely this kind of steady compounder, the re-escalated oil situation feeds straight into bitumen and therefore into the group's most profitable division, and positioning is complacent enough that the standing instruction is smaller adds and wider entry discounts. The catalyst here has already fired — the record order intake, the Oslofjord Link award and the NOK 11.25 dividend are all behind us — and in this book a spent catalyst is neither a plus nor a penalty; the case is judged on what is left. What is left is a narrow but real moat, concentrated in asphalt plants and quarries and in prequalification for large Norwegian civil works, at a price about 31% above what the parts are worth. Watch it rather than own it. The level that would make this interesting is the low NOK 130s, which is a genuine discount to the NOK 160 base value; the likelier route there is a bad third-quarter asphalt print or a project write-down, not a market wash-out, because a register with OBOS and Folketrygdfondet holding nearly 30% between them does not produce forced sellers.

interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic dossier — Veidekke ASA (VEI.OL)
**Date of review:** 2026-08-31 · **Price used:** NOK 210.00 (Oslo Børs, live quote) · **Shares outstanding:** 134,956,267

**A note on sources before anything else.** Veidekke does not publish an earnings-call transcript that our data vendor carries, and none could be located elsewhere. What follows is therefore built on primary documents rather than on a call: the company's own quarterly reports for the second quarter of 2026 (published 14 August 2026), the first quarter of 2026 (7 May 2026) and the fourth quarter of 2025 (12 February 2026), which carry management's written commentary and direct quotes from Group Chief Executive Jimmy Bengtsson, plus nine quarters of reported financials. Where this dossier quotes management, the quote comes from one of those reports and the report is named. No quote here is invented, and no figure is used that is not either in those reports, in the vendor's statement data, or in our own screener block.

Veidekke is Scandinavia's fourth-largest contractor: it builds buildings and infrastructure in Norway, Sweden and Denmark, and it also owns an asphalt-paving and aggregates (crushed rock and gravel) business in Norway and an industrial operation in Sweden. It sold its property-development arm years ago, so today it is a pure contractor plus that industrial tail. It employs 7,759 people.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

**The story has been the same one for six years, and — unusually — it has actually been delivered.**

In 2020 Veidekke launched a five-year strategy with one governing idea: profitability before growth. The concrete promise was a pre-tax profit margin (profit before tax divided by revenue) of 5% by 2025. The fourth-quarter 2025 report scores that promise itself, in management's own words: revenue rose 13% over the five years, from NOK 38.1 billion in 2020 to NOK 43.1 billion in 2025, while pre-tax profit rose 81%, from NOK 1.1 billion to NOK 2.1 billion, taking the margin from 3.0% to 4.8%. That is a company that deliberately declined to chase revenue and converted the restraint into profit. It is the opposite of the usual contractor arc, where a fat order book turns into a write-down two years later.

The arc since then is one of quiet extension rather than of pivot. The refreshed strategy for the years to 2030, set out in the same fourth-quarter 2025 report, keeps the shape and raises the bar slightly: a long-term pre-tax margin above 5%, annual revenue growth of 2.5 percentage points above market growth, and an unchanged dividend policy of distributing more than 70% of earnings per share. No new business line, no acquisition-led reinvention, no diversification into property development again. The only genuine addition to the story in the last two years is bolt-on buying in asphalt and aggregates — Euromining in northern Sweden (bought in late 2024, and it contributed NOK 740 million of revenue in 2025) and Nord Vei & Asfalt in Troms, northern Norway (bought 27 April 2026 for NOK 87 million, a business that earned NOK 38 million of operating profit on NOK 236 million of revenue in 2025). Management framed this itself in the first-quarter 2026 report, tying the balance sheet to the buying: the strong financial position "increases our acquisition capacity."

What has been quietly dropped is any pretence that the end market is good. The risk language has been essentially unchanged for a year and remains in the second-quarter 2026 report: weak sales of new homes, deferred or redesigned projects, and the expectation that construction-market conditions "remain challenging going forward." The tone lifted by exactly one adjective this quarter — the outlook has become "slightly more optimistic" — and no further.

**In one line:** the emphasis has moved from *fixing the margin* (2020–2024) to *proving the margin holds while volume comes back* (2025–2026), and the second quarter of 2026 is the strongest evidence yet that it does.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management's claim | Where it was made | What the numbers say | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| A 5% pre-tax margin by 2025 | 2020 strategy, scored in the Q4 2025 report | 4.8% for 2025; 5.0% for the twelve months to 30 June 2026 | Delivered, one year late by a rounding error |
| "All the business areas contributing to the group's growth" (Q2 2026) | Q2 2026 report | Every one of the five divisions grew both revenue and pre-tax profit year on year in the quarter; only Denmark's revenue was flat | Supported |
| "Solid revenue growth, higher profits and improved profitability" (Q2 2026) | Q2 2026 report | Revenue NOK 12.34bn, up 9%; pre-tax profit NOK 670m against NOK 538m, up 25%; margin 5.4% against 4.7% | Supported |
| "Our order intake is very high" (Q2 2026) | Q2 2026 report | Quarterly intake NOK 17.9bn against NOK 14.3bn; order book NOK 55.3bn, up from NOK 49.2bn a year earlier and NOK 47.3bn at year-end | Supported, and understated if anything |
| "Veidekke's solid financial position was further strengthened" (Q2 2026) | Q2 2026 report | Net interest-bearing assets NOK 3.65bn against NOK 1.24bn a year earlier — but *down* from NOK 4.02bn at year-end after a NOK 1.5bn dividend | Supported, with the honest caveat management supplied itself |
| Profitability in Construction Sweden "remains too low" | Q2 2026 report | That division earned 2.7% pre-tax over the last twelve months against a group 5.0%; it is the only division below its own 2024 profit | Management is telling the truth against itself |

**Three places where the narrative is *poorer* than the numbers, and management said so first.** This is the most striking forensic finding here: in every case where the reported result flattered the underlying business, the company flagged it in the same paragraph rather than letting it stand.

- The second quarter's operating cash flow of NOK 856 million (against negative NOK 167 million a year earlier) is described in the report as "partly attributable to a one-off advance of NOK 550 million received upon signature of Oslofjord Link contract." That is roughly two-thirds of the year-on-year swing, volunteered.
- The strong fourth quarter of 2025 in Infrastructure Sweden — NOK 202 million of the division's NOK 393 million full-year profit — is disclosed as including "a positive non-recurring effect of NOK 65 million linked to a reduction of the additional purchase price payable for Euromining." One third of that quarter's divisional profit was an accounting reversal on an earn-out, and they named it.
- The 2025 revenue increase of 4.2% is disclosed as including NOK 740 million from the Euromining acquisition — roughly 1.8 percentage points of it. Organic growth was closer to 2.4%.

**Two places where our own screener data is wrong, and the correction matters more than anything management said.**

- *The reported free cash flow is not distributable cash.* The screener shows a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 9.8 times and trailing free cash flow of NOK 4.44 billion, and the vendor's discounted-cash-flow model then produces a "fair value" of NOK 350. All three inherit the same flaw. In 2025 Veidekke reported NOK 3.29 billion of operating cash flow and NOK 2.89 billion of free cash flow, but that number contains a NOK 766 million working-capital inflow (customer money, not earned profit), charges only NOK 399 million of capital spending against NOK 1,099 million of depreciation, and excludes NOK 509 million of lease payments that sit in the financing section of the cash-flow statement. Strip those out and sustainable free cash is close to reported net profit — roughly NOK 1.6–1.7 billion — so the honest price-to-free-cash multiple at NOK 210 is about 17 times, not 9.8. **Any thesis built on "this thing trades at ten times cash flow" is built on a measurement artifact.**
- *The 100% gross margin is a feed error.* The vendor sets cost of revenue to zero in several quarters (in the first quarter of 2026 it reports gross profit identical to revenue). Veidekke's real gross margin is a few percent. Ignore the "gross margin expanding" line entirely.

**And one place where the business genuinely is remarkable.** Return on equity over the trailing twelve months is 56%, and return on invested capital is 20%. But read the equity ratio alongside it: 13% at 30 June 2026. Veidekke earns those returns because it runs on almost no capital — customers and suppliers fund the projects, and the company owns few assets beyond asphalt plants and equipment. That is a genuine feature of a well-run contractor and it is also why the return figure should not be read as pricing power.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising, from a low base, and disciplined about it.**

- *Fourth quarter 2025 (12 February 2026)* — the most confident language in the set, and it is retrospective rather than promissory: "2025 ended strongly, with increased revenues and higher profits than in Q4 of last year… The full-year profit margin is 4.8%, demonstrating the success of our improvement measures in recent years." The forward-looking content is a dividend proposal, not a forecast.
- *First quarter 2026 (7 May 2026)* — deliberately deflationary about a seasonally awful quarter, and specific about why: "The first quarter of the year is typically the low season for several of our operations, as reflected in both revenues and profit levels." Pre-tax profit that quarter was NOK 27 million on NOK 9.65 billion of revenue. Rather than dress it up, the report points at cost control through the low season and at the coming production season.
- *Second quarter 2026 (14 August 2026)* — the first genuinely offensive note in a while: "Veidekke had a strong second quarter… It is good to see all the business areas contributing to the group's growth. The asphalting season had a strong start."

The shift from defensive to offensive language is real but narrow. Even in the strongest quarter, the risk section still says the company "expects conditions in the construction market to remain challenging going forward." Management has not switched to a growth story; it has claimed a good quarter and left the market call alone.

**On specificity:** Veidekke gives no quarterly earnings guidance at all — it gives multi-year targets and then reports against them. That is unusual and, in a sector where guidance is routinely used to manage a share price, it is a point in the company's favour rather than against it. The one recurring forward disclosure is a Scandinavian contracting-market outlook published twice a year on the company's website.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: High.**

There is no quarter-by-quarter guidance to score, so the test has to be the multi-year targets, and those are unusually testable because they were set publicly in 2020 with a date on them.

| Promise | Made | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 5% pre-tax margin by 2025 | 2020 five-year strategy | 4.8% in 2025; 5.0% for the twelve months to June 2026 |
| Profitability prioritised over growth | 2020 | Revenue +13% over five years while pre-tax profit +81% — exactly the trade they described |
| Distribute more than 70% of earnings per share | Standing policy | NOK 9.00 per share for 2024 (NOK 1,215m, paid May 2025); NOK 11.25 for 2025 (NOK 1,518m, approved at the annual general meeting on 6 May 2026 and paid in the second quarter of 2026) — roughly 98% of 2025 earnings per share of NOK 11.50 |
| Zero serious injuries | 2020 | **Not achieved**, and the company says so plainly in the Q4 2025 report. Two serious injuries in the fourth quarter of 2025, one in the second quarter of 2026, and the lost-time-injury rate has worsened to 3.8 from 2.4 a year ago |

Our screener's earnings-beat rate of five in seven quarters, or 71%, is consistent with a company that under-promises: analyst coverage in the vendor data is only two estimates deep, and their 2025 consensus earnings per share of NOK 10.22 came in 12% below the NOK 11.50 actually delivered. There is a sandbagging pattern, but it is a *coverage* artifact as much as a management one — a thinly-followed Norwegian mid-cap whose two forecasters keep running behind the print.

**The one credibility blemish is safety, not accounting**, and the company reports it rather than burying it. In a business where serious incidents cause project shutdowns and prequalification problems, that trend deserves watching in its own right.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

With no call transcript there is no question-and-answer record to mine, so this section is necessarily inference from what the reports choose to volunteer — which is itself informative, because companies pre-empt the questions they expect.

- **Construction Sweden.** Volunteered every quarter and never resolved. It earned 2.7% pre-tax over the last twelve months on NOK 7.9 billion of revenue, against 10.2% in Denmark on less than half the revenue. The Q2 2026 report concedes that outside the Gothenburg subsidiary BRA, "profitability of other operations within Construction Sweden remains too low." Six years into a profitability-first strategy, one fifth of the group's revenue still is not fixed.
- **The Infrastructure Sweden order book.** Down 19% year on year in local currency, to NOK 7.0 billion — the only division whose backlog is shrinking, and it happens to be the division that produced the largest margin improvement. That combination (best margin, worst order intake) is the classic set-up for a division earning well on a book that is running out.
- **Bitumen.** The report devotes a full paragraph to it: Middle East turmoil has pushed up oil and energy prices and therefore the price of bitumen, the binder in asphalt. Public-sector contracts contain adjustment mechanisms that "largely" cover the price, but the price rises squeeze public asphalt budgets and private demand, and the company says outright there is "uncertainty about asphalt volumes in 2026." Veidekke has contracted just over 770,000 tonnes for this year's public tenders, significantly more than last year, but those contracts permit volume changes of up to 15% either way.
- **Project concentration.** The single biggest new order — the E134 Oslofjord Link for the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, NOK 5.5 billion — is a large, technically demanding subsea road-tunnel project. Nothing in the reports addresses how its risk is contained. For a company whose whole equity base is NOK 2.6 billion, one contract worth twice that is the thing a director must think about.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **Margins are at the top of their own range, not in the middle of it.** The 5.0% trailing pre-tax margin is the target the company set for itself as an *ambition* six years ago; the ten-year history sits at 3–4.5%. Our screener puts the current margin 1.27 standard deviations from its historical peak. Valuing this business off the current margin is valuing it at the good end of its cycle.
- **Infrastructure Sweden's order book fell 19% in local currency** (second quarter 2026) while its margin rose to 5.9%.
- **The first quarter is structurally near-breakeven and always will be.** Infrastructure Norway lost NOK 207 million before tax in the first quarter of 2026 and NOK 189 million in the first quarter of 2025, because asphalt does not get laid in a Norwegian winter. Group earnings per share for that quarter were NOK 0.10.
- **Safety is going the wrong way:** lost-time-injury rate 3.8 against 2.4 a year earlier, with a serious injury in the quarter.
- **No insider buying** (our screener records an insider buy ratio of zero), though roughly 10% of the company is owned by employees, which is a different and better kind of alignment.
- **The equity cushion is thin by design.** A 13% equity ratio at 30 June 2026 means a single large loss-making project consumes a visible share of book value.

**Green flags**

- **A publicly dated six-year promise, delivered.** Margin from 3.0% to 4.8%–5.0%, with growth deliberately forgone.
- **A record order book of NOK 55.3 billion**, up 12.5% year on year and up 17% since year-end, of which NOK 30.5 billion converts to revenue within twelve months.
- **Genuine net cash of NOK 3.65 billion** at 30 June 2026 — after paying a NOK 1.5 billion dividend — with NOK 3.0 billion of committed bank facilities entirely undrawn (a NOK 2.0 billion overdraft with DNB to February 2030 and a NOK 1.0 billion facility with Nordea to February 2028).
- **Disclosure quality is high and self-critical.** The one-off cash advance, the earn-out reversal, the acquisition contribution to revenue, the Swedish underperformance and the missed safety target are all volunteered by the company, not dug out of the notes.
- **Bolt-on acquisitions are being made at genuinely low prices.** Nord Vei & Asfalt cost NOK 87 million for a business that earned NOK 38 million of operating profit in 2025 — a little over two times operating profit, in a segment where Veidekke already has plants and routes to exploit.
- **The dividend is real and rising:** NOK 9.00 for 2024, NOK 11.25 for 2025, both fully paid in cash from operating profit.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

- **The language around the balance sheet changed function.** For years the net cash position was described defensively, as resilience. In the first quarter of 2026 it acquired a purpose: it "increases our acquisition capacity." Two asphalt and aggregates acquisitions have followed inside twelve months (Nord Vei & Asfalt in April, a proposed purchase of Ucklum Grus AB in Sweden still being updated as of 28 August 2026), plus a small Danish deal. Veidekke is quietly converting a contractor's cash pile into an industrial-materials footprint — the one part of the group with local, physical barriers to entry.
- **Where the profit actually comes from is drifting.** Over the last twelve months, asphalt and aggregates earned 6.7% pre-tax and Denmark 10.2%, against 4.6% in Norwegian civil engineering and 2.7% in Swedish building. The parts of Veidekke that look least like general contracting are carrying an increasing share of the profit.
- **A "long-term" margin target replaced a dated one.** The 2020 strategy said 5% *by 2025*. The 2030 strategy says a *long-term* margin *above* 5%. Slightly higher, and no longer attached to a year — a small softening of accountability that no one will notice for four years.
- **The growth target is expressed relative to the market**, not in absolute terms: 2.5 percentage points above market growth. In a shrinking market that target is compatible with shrinking.
- **The shareholder register is built to sit still.** OBOS, a Norwegian housing cooperative, owns 19.5%; the state-linked Folketrygdfondet owns 9.8%; the top ten hold 49.3%; foreign holders are only 17.7%. Roughly 10% of shares are employee-owned. This is a register that neither panics nor squeezes.
- **The share has already moved.** The report records a second-quarter trading range of NOK 170.80 to NOK 197.60 and a 30 June close of NOK 189.60. The live price on 31 August 2026 is NOK 210 — up 11% since quarter-end, against a 52-week low of NOK 152.60 and a 52-week high of NOK 211. The market has read the same report we have.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Every division improved profit year on year in the second quarter of 2026; the order book is at a record; the balance sheet has net cash after a near-100%-payout dividend; and the six-year margin promise has been kept. There is no forensic reason to distrust these accounts. If anything, the company is more candid about its own soft spots than most.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** *You are being asked to pay a top-of-range multiple for a top-of-range margin, and the screener's cheapness signal is a measurement error.* At NOK 210 the shares trade at roughly 16.8 times the last twelve months' earnings per share of NOK 12.50, and about 15 times once the net cash of NOK 27 per share is set aside — for a business earning a 5.0% pre-tax margin, which is the best margin in its own recorded history and the exact number it set as a stretch ambition six years ago. The "9.8 times free cash flow" that put this name on the screen dissolves on inspection: adjusted for the working-capital inflow, the under-spend on capital expenditure against depreciation, and the lease payments booked below the free-cash line, the real multiple of sustainable cash is around 17 times. So the question is not "is this cheap and good?" — it is "does a bid-market contractor at a cyclical margin peak deserve fifteen times?" Everything else is secondary to that.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and stable.** The moat type is best described as local scale-cost plus regulatory prequalification. It is genuine in two places: asphalt and aggregates, where plants, quarries and haulage radius create real local pricing power (and where Veidekke is actively buying more of it at two to three times operating profit), and large Norwegian civil works, where a short list of contractors is prequalified for state road and rail tenders. Everywhere else — building in Norway, Sweden and Denmark — the work is won bid by bid at 3–5% margins, which is the honest measure of how much pricing power exists. On the evidence, returns are rising (return on equity 44% to 56% over two years; return on invested capital 20%; margin 3.0% to 5.0% since 2020), and a mechanical reading of rising returns with expanding margins would call this widening. It should not be read that way: the improvement came from project selection, capacity utilisation and cost discipline inside an unchanged competitive structure, and the headline return on equity is flattered by a 13% equity ratio. Call it narrow and holding its width.

**Secular threat: manageable, not terminal.** No structural force is eroding the demand for Scandinavian roads, rail, schools and homes; public infrastructure and road-maintenance spending is durable and the order book says so. The genuine pressures — a 19-year-high long-end interest rate suppressing private housing starts, and bitumen costs rising with oil while Hormuz stays contested — are cyclical input and demand pressures with contractual pass-through mechanisms, not a melting terminal value. The cheapness signal here is therefore neither a fear-print nor a value trap: it is simply not cheapness at all once the cash-flow measurement is corrected. This is a good business at a full price, which is a different problem from a bad business at a low one.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

bull_thesis: Veidekke is a genuinely well-run Scandinavian contractor that did exactly what it said it would do, and the second quarter of 2026 was its best evidence yet. Back in 2020 the company set a single public promise: put profitability ahead of growth and reach a 5% pre-tax profit margin (profit before tax divided by revenue) by 2025. It scored itself in the fourth-quarter 2025 report published on 12 February 2026: revenue up 13% over five years, from NOK 38.1 billion to NOK 43.1 billion, while pre-tax profit rose 81%, from NOK 1.1 billion to NOK 2.1 billion, lifting the margin from 3.0% to 4.8%. By the twelve months to 30 June 2026 the margin was 5.0% — the promise, kept. The second quarter itself, reported on 14 August 2026, showed revenue of NOK 12.3 billion (up 9% on the year), pre-tax profit of NOK 670 million (up 25%), and a 5.4% margin, with every one of the five divisions improving both revenue and profit. Behind that sits a record order book of NOK 55.3 billion at 30 June, up from NOK 49.2 billion a year earlier and NOK 47.3 billion at year-end, of which NOK 30.5 billion converts to revenue within twelve months. Quarterly order intake of NOK 17.9 billion included a NOK 5.5 billion contract for the E134 Oslofjord Link from the Norwegian Public Roads Administration. The balance sheet is the other half of the case: net interest-bearing assets of NOK 3.65 billion at 30 June, and that is after paying out NOK 1.5 billion of dividend during the quarter, with NOK 3.0 billion of committed bank facilities entirely undrawn. The stated policy is to distribute more than 70% of earnings per share, and the company has: NOK 9.00 per share for 2024 and NOK 11.25 for 2025, which at NOK 210 is a yield of about 5.4%. Management is using the cash rather than hoarding it — buying local asphalt and aggregates businesses at strikingly low prices, including Nord Vei & Asfalt in Troms on 27 April 2026 for NOK 87 million, a business that made NOK 38 million of operating profit on NOK 236 million of revenue in 2025, a little over two times operating profit. That matters strategically: asphalt, quarries and haulage radius are the one part of a contractor that has real local pricing power, and Veidekke is steadily buying more of it. Over the last twelve months asphalt and aggregates earned a 6.7% pre-tax margin and Denmark 10.2%, against 4.6% in Norwegian civil engineering — the mix is drifting toward the better businesses. The conditions the bull case needs: that the record order book converts at the current margin rather than at the lower margin of the work being replaced; that Swedish building, at a 2.7% margin over the last twelve months, is finally fixed toward the 4% the company thinks it should earn; that bitumen costs stay passed through; and that the market keeps paying thirteen to fifteen times for it. If all four hold, earnings power of roughly NOK 15 to NOK 16 per share by 2027 at fourteen times, plus the net cash, is worth about NOK 235 a share — and the shareholder collects a 5-6% dividend while waiting.
bear_thesis: The bear case is not that Veidekke is a bad company. It is that you are being asked to pay a top-of-range price for a top-of-range margin, and that the number which flagged this stock as cheap is a measurement error. Start with the error. Our screener shows a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 9.8 times, trailing free cash flow of NOK 4.44 billion, and a model-derived fair value of NOK 350 — and all three inherit the same flaw. In 2025 Veidekke reported NOK 2.89 billion of free cash flow, but that figure contains a NOK 766 million working-capital inflow (customer money, not earned profit), charges only NOK 399 million of capital spending against NOK 1,099 million of depreciation, and excludes NOK 509 million of lease payments booked in the financing section of the cash-flow statement. Correct all three and sustainable free cash is close to reported net profit — roughly NOK 1.6 to NOK 1.7 billion — so the honest multiple of distributable cash at NOK 210 is about seventeen times, not under ten. Even the second quarter's strong operating cash flow of NOK 856 million is disclosed by the company itself as helped by a one-off NOK 550 million advance received on signing the Oslofjord Link contract. On earnings the picture is the same: NOK 210 is 16.8 times the last twelve months' earnings per share of NOK 12.50, or roughly fifteen times once the NOK 27 per share of net cash is set aside. That would be an ordinary multiple for a business with pricing power. Veidekke does not have much: outside asphalt and quarries, it wins work bid by bid at 3 to 5 percent margins, which is the honest measure of its bargaining position. The 56% return on equity is not evidence to the contrary — it is arithmetic on a 13% equity ratio, because customers and suppliers fund the projects. And the margin being capitalised is the best in the company's recorded history. Our own screener puts it 1.27 standard deviations from its historic peak; the ten-year range is 3 to 4.5 percent. Denmark at 10.2% and Infrastructure Sweden at 5.9% over the last twelve months are both well above their own long-run levels, and Infrastructure Sweden's order book fell 19% in local currency year on year — the best margin sitting on the worst backlog. Three specific things can break it. First, bitumen: the second-quarter report gives a full paragraph to Middle East turmoil pushing up oil and therefore bitumen, states that price rises squeeze public asphalt budgets and private demand, and concedes 'uncertainty about asphalt volumes in 2026'; the contracts allow volume to move up or down by 15%. Second, one project: the group's entire equity is NOK 2.6 billion and its largest new contract is NOK 5.5 billion of technically demanding subsea tunnelling — contractors do not die of slow decline, they die of one job. Third, the multiple: the same shares traded between NOK 170.80 and NOK 197.60 during the second quarter and closed the quarter at NOK 189.60, with a 52-week low of NOK 152.60. Nothing structural stops them going back. If margins revert to the 4.1% of 2024 and the market pays ten times, the shares are worth about NOK 105. That is the risk being taken for an upside that, on today's segment earnings, the price has already reached.
consensus_delta: There are two disagreements with the market here and they point in opposite directions, which is why the answer is a pass rather than a short. The first disagreement is in the company's favour and it is about the near-term numbers. Analyst coverage of this share is extremely thin — the estimate data carries only two forecasters — and they have been running behind the print. Their 2025 consensus earnings per share was NOK 10.22 against NOK 11.50 actually delivered, a 12% miss. For 2026 they carry NOK 12.41, but the first half already produced NOK 3.80 against NOK 2.80 a year earlier, a 36% increase, and the second half of the year is seasonally where this company makes its money. On an unchanged second-half growth rate the full year lands nearer NOK 13.30 to NOK 13.50. So near-term estimates are more likely to go up than down, and anyone expecting a disappointing print in November is probably wrong. The second disagreement is against the company and it is the one that decides the capital call. It is not about earnings at all — it is about what those earnings are worth. Consensus has revenue reaching NOK 51.3 billion by 2028 and earnings per share of NOK 13.79, which is barely 3.5% annual growth from the 2026 level, and at NOK 210 the market is paying fifteen times that, net of cash, for a business whose margin is already the best in its recorded history. The market assumption embedded in that price is that a 5% pre-tax margin is the new normal rather than the top of a range. The evidence says otherwise: the ten-year history runs at 3 to 4.5 percent, our screener puts the current margin 1.27 standard deviations from its historic peak, Denmark at 10.2% and Infrastructure Sweden at 5.9% over the last twelve months are both far above their own long-run levels, and Infrastructure Sweden's order book is down 19% in local currency — the highest margin sitting on the fastest-shrinking backlog. A second market assumption is embedded in how this name reached our screen at all: the reported free cash flow of NOK 4.44 billion, and the 9.8 times cash-flow multiple derived from it, are not distributable cash. They contain a NOK 766 million working-capital inflow, charge NOK 399 million of capital spending against NOK 1,099 million of depreciation, and exclude NOK 509 million of lease payments booked below the line. Corrected, the multiple of sustainable cash is about seventeen times. The market is not looking the wrong way on this company. If anything, it is looking at it rather carefully, which is why the shares sit at a 52-week high.
forcing_function: There is no event that forces the market to re-rate these shares upward, because the re-rating already happened. The dates that matter now are tests of a best-ever margin rather than catalysts for it. The third-quarter 2026 results are due in early November (the equivalent 2025 report was published on 6 November 2025) and will show whether the asphalt season's 17% volume gain survived contact with higher bitumen costs — that is the single most informative print in the next six months. The full-year 2026 results are due in mid-February 2027 (the 2025 equivalent was 12 February 2026) and will carry the board's dividend proposal under the more-than-70%-of-earnings policy; on a full-year figure near NOK 13.30 that implies something in the region of NOK 12 to NOK 13 per share, payable after the annual general meeting in early May 2027. Veidekke also publishes a Scandinavian contracting-market outlook twice a year on its own website, which is the closest thing this company offers to guidance. The genuine forcing function on the downside is different in kind and has no date attached: a single loss-making project. The group's entire equity is NOK 2.6 billion and its largest new contract, the NOK 5.5 billion E134 Oslofjord Link subsea tunnel, is more than twice that. Contractors re-rate violently on one job, in either direction, and nothing in the current disclosure lets an outsider judge how that risk is contained.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months contain no crisis, but they do contain a reliable de-rating window and two live cost pressures. The reliable window is seasonal and structural. Veidekke's first quarter is close to breakeven every single year, because asphalt is not laid in a Norwegian winter: Infrastructure Norway lost NOK 207 million before tax in the first quarter of 2026 and NOK 189 million in the first quarter of 2025, and group earnings per share for the first quarter of 2026 were NOK 0.10 against minus NOK 0.20 a year before. A share trading at nearly seventeen times trailing earnings has to walk through that print every February to May, and it does so immediately after the full-year dividend has been declared but before it has been paid. The first live pressure is bitumen, the oil-derived binder in asphalt. The second-quarter report devotes a paragraph to it: Middle East turmoil has pushed up oil and energy prices and therefore bitumen; public-sector contracts contain adjustment mechanisms that only 'largely' cover it; price rises squeeze public asphalt budgets and private demand; and the company states plainly that there is uncertainty about asphalt volumes for 2026. Veidekke has contracted just over 770,000 tonnes in this year's public tenders, well up on last year, but those contracts allow volumes to move 15% either way. With Brent around NOK-equivalent highs and the Hormuz situation re-escalated as of the mid-August market read, this is a real and dated squeeze on the single most profitable part of the group, and it will be visible in the third-quarter report in early November — the quarter that contains the peak of the paving season. The second pressure is the cost of money. Long-term interest rates are at a nineteen-year high, and Veidekke's own risk section says higher rates are cutting the financial capacity of both private and public clients, producing weak new-home sales and deferred or redesigned projects; management still expects construction market conditions to remain challenging. That does not hit the order book already signed, but it decides what replaces it. Finally, cash. The net position fell from NOK 4.02 billion at year-end to NOK 3.65 billion at 30 June after the NOK 1.5 billion dividend, and the second quarter's operating inflow was helped by a NOK 550 million one-off advance on the Oslofjord Link. As that project consumes its advance and the big civil works burn working capital, the cash figure that makes the balance sheet look impregnable will drift lower — not dangerously, but enough that anyone underwriting the full NOK 27 a share of net cash as permanent will be disappointed. There is no debt wall: total interest-bearing liabilities are NOK 170 million and NOK 3.0 billion of bank facilities sit undrawn.
positioning_washout: There is no forced-selling opportunity here, and that is itself the finding. The share register is built to sit still. As at 30 June 2026, OBOS, a Norwegian housing cooperative, held 19.5% and the state-linked Folketrygdfondet 9.8% — nearly 30% in two hands that do not trade. The ten largest holders account for 49.3%, foreign ownership is only 17.7%, and roughly 10% of the company is owned by its own employees. Just 4.6 million shares changed hands in the whole of the second quarter, against 135 million outstanding. This is a domestic, income-oriented, long-duration register: it will not panic into your bid, and it will not squeeze a short either. The one mechanical scenario that would move it is a dividend cut. Veidekke's stated policy is to distribute more than 70% of earnings per share, and it has been paying closer to 100% — NOK 11.25 for 2025 against earnings of NOK 11.50. A significant share of the register owns this specifically for that yield, so a cut, which would only come from a large loss-making project or a genuine margin break, would produce real mechanical selling from income funds. That is the entry this name is most likely to hand you, and it is not on the calendar. The practical conclusion for timing: do not wait for a wash-out that the ownership structure cannot produce. If this is ever bought, it will be bought into a bad print, not into a liquidation.
moderator_conclusion: Pass for now — a good business at a full price. Almost everything about Veidekke's operating record is admirable, and the forensic review found no reason to distrust the accounts: the company set a public five-year target in 2020 to lift its pre-tax profit margin to 5%, deliberately gave up growth to get there, and delivered 4.8% in 2025 and 5.0% over the twelve months to June 2026. Every division improved in the second quarter of 2026, the order book is a record NOK 55.3 billion, there is NOK 3.65 billion of net cash after a NOK 1.5 billion dividend, and management discloses its own soft spots — the one-off cash advance, the earn-out reversal, the acquisition contribution to revenue, the too-low Swedish margin and the missed safety target — rather than burying them. That earns a high credibility mark. The problem is entirely one of price, and it starts with the reason this name reached the screen at all. The 9.8-times free-cash-flow signal is a measurement error: strip out the working-capital inflow, charge depreciation-level capital spending instead of the NOK 399 million actually spent, and put the NOK 509 million of lease payments back where they belong, and sustainable free cash is close to reported profit — about seventeen times the current price, not under ten. The model-derived fair value of NOK 350 inherits the same flaw and should be discarded. On corrected numbers, NOK 210 is 16.8 times the last twelve months' earnings of NOK 12.50, or roughly fifteen times net of the NOK 27 a share of net cash, for a company earning the best margin in its recorded history in a business where work is won bid by bid at 3 to 5 percent. Valuing the divisions separately on normalised margins gives NOK 160 a share; valuing them on today's margins with a generous multiple and the full cash gives NOK 209 — which is to say the market price already contains the good case. The adverse case, a reversion to 2024 margins at ten times, is NOK 105. Reading this against the current market backdrop reinforces rather than changes the call: this is not a thesis that depends on rate cuts, and its driver — Scandinavian construction demand and Norwegian public works budgets — is genuinely independent of the crowded macro trades, which is a point in its favour. But long-term interest rates at a nineteen-year high raise the discount rate on precisely this kind of steady compounder, the re-escalated oil situation feeds straight into bitumen and therefore into the group's most profitable division, and positioning is complacent enough that the standing instruction is smaller adds and wider entry discounts. The catalyst here has already fired — the record order intake, the Oslofjord Link award and the NOK 11.25 dividend are all behind us — and in this book a spent catalyst is neither a plus nor a penalty; the case is judged on what is left. What is left is a narrow but real moat, concentrated in asphalt plants and quarries and in prequalification for large Norwegian civil works, at a price about 31% above what the parts are worth. Watch it rather than own it. The level that would make this interesting is the low NOK 130s, which is a genuine discount to the NOK 160 base value; the likelier route there is a bad third-quarter asphalt print or a project write-down, not a market wash-out, because a register with OBOS and Folketrygdfondet holding nearly 30% between them does not produce forced sellers.
sop_breakdown: Base case, valuing each division on a normalised margin taxed at 23% and capitalised at twelve times after-tax profit (fourteen times for asphalt and aggregates, which has genuine local scale), then adding a haircut cash position. Construction Norway at a 4.5% margin on NOK 15.8bn of revenue: NOK 6.6bn. Infrastructure Norway civil engineering at 4.5% on NOK 6.3bn: NOK 2.6bn. Asphalt and aggregates at 6.0% on NOK 4.2bn: NOK 2.7bn. Construction Sweden at its current 2.7% on NOK 7.9bn, because six years of trying have not fixed it: NOK 1.8bn. Infrastructure Sweden at 5.0% on NOK 7.6bn, below the 5.9% it earned last year because its order book is down 19% in local currency: NOK 3.5bn. Denmark at 8.5% on NOK 3.6bn, below its 10.2%: NOK 2.8bn. Corporate costs: minus NOK 1.6bn. The operating parts sum to about NOK 18.4bn. Net interest-bearing assets were NOK 3.65bn at 30 June 2026, but roughly NOK 0.6bn of that is the one-off contract advance the company disclosed and the position swings with customer money through the year, so NOK 3.0bn is credited. Total about NOK 21.4bn across 134,956,267 shares, or NOK 159 — call it NOK 160. The same answer arrives from the top down: normalised core earnings of about NOK 11 a share at twelve times, plus NOK 22 a share of credited net cash.
risk_reward: Unattractive at NOK 210. The base-case value of the parts is NOK 160, so the shares trade about 31% above what the business is worth on normalised divisional margins, and the favourable case built on today's divisional earnings arrives at roughly NOK 209 — the market price. The adverse case, in which margins revert to their 2024 level and the multiple compresses to ten times, is NOK 105. So the shape is roughly NOK 105 below against NOK 235 above, entered at NOK 210: the whole of the ordinary case is already in the price, and the shareholder is left holding the tail. The 5.4% dividend yield is a comfort while waiting but it is not a floor — a contractor's payout is the first thing cut if a large project goes wrong, and it is not a contractual entitlement.
peer_comps_note: The peer file compares Veidekke with the other large Nordic contractors — AF Gruppen, Skanska, Peab and NCC, with JM as a residential-development comparison — and its verdict is that Veidekke sits in line with them, not at a discount. It carries no live peer multiple to anchor against, and no current peer multiple is quoted here from memory, because stale comparison multiples are exactly how a fake discount gets manufactured. The peer note's own reasoning is worth repeating because it agrees with ours from a different direction: Veidekke's standout figures — earnings per share up 23.7%, a 20% return on invested capital well above the Nordic contractor norm, a solvency score of 3.5 — largely explain and already reflect the modest valuation gap the screener flagged, and with the share essentially at its 52-week high, re-rating room looks limited rather than this being a fresh mispricing. The multiples used in the valuation above are therefore anchored on the company's own history and on the economics of each division (twelve times after-tax profit for bid-market contracting, fourteen for asphalt and aggregates where local plants and quarries create real pricing power), not on a peer print. One relative-value observation does stand on its own: the group's blend of a 5.0% pre-tax margin and a fifteen-times multiple net of cash is a top-of-range combination on both axes at once, which is the classic way a cyclical looks cheap and is not.
interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic dossier — Veidekke ASA (VEI.OL)
**Date of review:** 2026-08-31 · **Price used:** NOK 210.00 (Oslo Børs, live quote) · **Shares outstanding:** 134,956,267

**A note on sources before anything else.** Veidekke does not publish an earnings-call transcript that our data vendor carries, and none could be located elsewhere. What follows is therefore built on primary documents rather than on a call: the company's own quarterly reports for the second quarter of 2026 (published 14 August 2026), the first quarter of 2026 (7 May 2026) and the fourth quarter of 2025 (12 February 2026), which carry management's written commentary and direct quotes from Group Chief Executive Jimmy Bengtsson, plus nine quarters of reported financials. Where this dossier quotes management, the quote comes from one of those reports and the report is named. No quote here is invented, and no figure is used that is not either in those reports, in the vendor's statement data, or in our own screener block.

Veidekke is Scandinavia's fourth-largest contractor: it builds buildings and infrastructure in Norway, Sweden and Denmark, and it also owns an asphalt-paving and aggregates (crushed rock and gravel) business in Norway and an industrial operation in Sweden. It sold its property-development arm years ago, so today it is a pure contractor plus that industrial tail. It employs 7,759 people.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

**The story has been the same one for six years, and — unusually — it has actually been delivered.**

In 2020 Veidekke launched a five-year strategy with one governing idea: profitability before growth. The concrete promise was a pre-tax profit margin (profit before tax divided by revenue) of 5% by 2025. The fourth-quarter 2025 report scores that promise itself, in management's own words: revenue rose 13% over the five years, from NOK 38.1 billion in 2020 to NOK 43.1 billion in 2025, while pre-tax profit rose 81%, from NOK 1.1 billion to NOK 2.1 billion, taking the margin from 3.0% to 4.8%. That is a company that deliberately declined to chase revenue and converted the restraint into profit. It is the opposite of the usual contractor arc, where a fat order book turns into a write-down two years later.

The arc since then is one of quiet extension rather than of pivot. The refreshed strategy for the years to 2030, set out in the same fourth-quarter 2025 report, keeps the shape and raises the bar slightly: a long-term pre-tax margin above 5%, annual revenue growth of 2.5 percentage points above market growth, and an unchanged dividend policy of distributing more than 70% of earnings per share. No new business line, no acquisition-led reinvention, no diversification into property development again. The only genuine addition to the story in the last two years is bolt-on buying in asphalt and aggregates — Euromining in northern Sweden (bought in late 2024, and it contributed NOK 740 million of revenue in 2025) and Nord Vei & Asfalt in Troms, northern Norway (bought 27 April 2026 for NOK 87 million, a business that earned NOK 38 million of operating profit on NOK 236 million of revenue in 2025). Management framed this itself in the first-quarter 2026 report, tying the balance sheet to the buying: the strong financial position "increases our acquisition capacity."

What has been quietly dropped is any pretence that the end market is good. The risk language has been essentially unchanged for a year and remains in the second-quarter 2026 report: weak sales of new homes, deferred or redesigned projects, and the expectation that construction-market conditions "remain challenging going forward." The tone lifted by exactly one adjective this quarter — the outlook has become "slightly more optimistic" — and no further.

**In one line:** the emphasis has moved from *fixing the margin* (2020–2024) to *proving the margin holds while volume comes back* (2025–2026), and the second quarter of 2026 is the strongest evidence yet that it does.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management's claim | Where it was made | What the numbers say | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| A 5% pre-tax margin by 2025 | 2020 strategy, scored in the Q4 2025 report | 4.8% for 2025; 5.0% for the twelve months to 30 June 2026 | Delivered, one year late by a rounding error |
| "All the business areas contributing to the group's growth" (Q2 2026) | Q2 2026 report | Every one of the five divisions grew both revenue and pre-tax profit year on year in the quarter; only Denmark's revenue was flat | Supported |
| "Solid revenue growth, higher profits and improved profitability" (Q2 2026) | Q2 2026 report | Revenue NOK 12.34bn, up 9%; pre-tax profit NOK 670m against NOK 538m, up 25%; margin 5.4% against 4.7% | Supported |
| "Our order intake is very high" (Q2 2026) | Q2 2026 report | Quarterly intake NOK 17.9bn against NOK 14.3bn; order book NOK 55.3bn, up from NOK 49.2bn a year earlier and NOK 47.3bn at year-end | Supported, and understated if anything |
| "Veidekke's solid financial position was further strengthened" (Q2 2026) | Q2 2026 report | Net interest-bearing assets NOK 3.65bn against NOK 1.24bn a year earlier — but *down* from NOK 4.02bn at year-end after a NOK 1.5bn dividend | Supported, with the honest caveat management supplied itself |
| Profitability in Construction Sweden "remains too low" | Q2 2026 report | That division earned 2.7% pre-tax over the last twelve months against a group 5.0%; it is the only division below its own 2024 profit | Management is telling the truth against itself |

**Three places where the narrative is *poorer* than the numbers, and management said so first.** This is the most striking forensic finding here: in every case where the reported result flattered the underlying business, the company flagged it in the same paragraph rather than letting it stand.

- The second quarter's operating cash flow of NOK 856 million (against negative NOK 167 million a year earlier) is described in the report as "partly attributable to a one-off advance of NOK 550 million received upon signature of Oslofjord Link contract." That is roughly two-thirds of the year-on-year swing, volunteered.
- The strong fourth quarter of 2025 in Infrastructure Sweden — NOK 202 million of the division's NOK 393 million full-year profit — is disclosed as including "a positive non-recurring effect of NOK 65 million linked to a reduction of the additional purchase price payable for Euromining." One third of that quarter's divisional profit was an accounting reversal on an earn-out, and they named it.
- The 2025 revenue increase of 4.2% is disclosed as including NOK 740 million from the Euromining acquisition — roughly 1.8 percentage points of it. Organic growth was closer to 2.4%.

**Two places where our own screener data is wrong, and the correction matters more than anything management said.**
